Definition: properly, something round (as excavated or bored), i.e. a chafing-dish for coals or a caldron for cooking; hence (from similarity of form) a washbowl; also (for the same reason) a pulpit or platform
KeyPassages: Exodus 30:18; Leviticus 8:11; 1 Samuel 2:14; 1 Kings 7:30; 2 Kings 16:17; 2 Chronicles 4:6
BiblicalUsage: Kiyor is a laver, a great round vessel for washing, and also the caldron and the platform of the same round shape. Exodus 30:18 commands a laver of brass to wash withal, set between the tabernacle and the altar, Leviticus 8:11 anoints the laver and his foot to sanctify them, and 2 Chronicles 4:6 makes ten lavers to wash the burnt offerings in. 1 Samuel 2:14 shows the other sense, the caldron into which the fleshhook strikes for the priest's portion, and 1 Kings 7:30 and 2 Kings 16:17 describe the lavers on their bases in Solomon's temple, until Ahaz cuts off their borders.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe the laver stands between the altar and the tent for a reason: no priest comes to God without washing first. I hold that the water in the laver is the Old Testament's picture of the washing the New Testament promises, and Ahaz cutting it down is what happens when kings stop valuing it.
RelatedBooks: Exodus; Leviticus; 1 Samuel; 1 Kings; 2 Kings; 2 Chronicles
